De wakk're **WILLEM**, Prins van 't wydberoemde Oranje,
Die Nederland verlofte, in wederwil van Spanje,
Van 't onverdraaglyk juk der slaafsche dwinglandy,
En uit de banden der Gewetenstiranny.
De wetenschappen zyn in uwen kreits herboren.
Gamaliëls doen zich in u geduurig hooren,
En teelen, niet alleen voor Kerk, en Stad en Staat,
Maar voor al de Aarde een reeks van Mannen, vroeg en laat;
Van Mannen, die uw roem hoe langs hoe meer doen groeijen.
Steeds moet ge, ô Hooge School! door Letterhelden bloeijen,
Wier lof de lof verdooft, gelyk zy altoos deed,
Van al wat ooit zyn vlyt den Lett'ren heeft besteed.
Nu lust het my de **KERK VAN PIETER** te bekyken.
Dit Kerkgesticht behoeft in schoonheid niet te wyken
Voor een gebouw waar mede een Stad in Holland praalt.
Zyn pracht en luister, daar 't nieuwsgierig oog in dwaalt,
Bekoort me! langen tyd moet het zyn stant behouwen.
De **KERK VAN 'T HOOGELAND**, een uwer Hoofdgebouwen
ô Leyden! dryft me voort: Daar zie ik 't fraai gesticht,
Dat voor vier eeuwen kwam zo heerlyk in het licht!
Zyn luister, zwier en stant kan mynen geest behaagen.
De **LIEVEVROUWE KERK**, die laater op kwam dagen,
En kleener is, behoeft in netheid en sieraad,
Ook niet te zwichten voor een Kerk van Neêrlands Staat.
Ik ga naar 't **GASTHUIS** toe, genaamd na Sint **KATRYNE**:
Hier word den zieken, moede en afgemat door pyne,
Verkwikt, gekoestert en geneezen en hersteld;
En hem, die d' Armoede in zyn banden houd beknelt,
Word hier verzadigt, en voorzien met dak en kleeren,
Terwyl de Kerk hen dient, om 't waare woord des Heeren
Te hooren, op dat dus de ziel, zo min als 't lyf,
Haar voedzel derve, en niet om troost verlegen blyf.
Steeds moet de liefde tot elks nut uw hart doen blaaken,
ô Leydsburgery! zo zal de Godheid waaken
Voor 't welzyn van uw Stad, en Godsdienst, als voorheen.
Nu eens 't **BEGGYNHOF** van de Maagden ingetreen,
Die, naar de Roomsche wyz', de Kerk, haar kuisheid weyden,
Of eer, uit Bygeloof, een eenzaam leeven leyden;
Zyn stant is lustig; en de **KERK**, die 't Hof verfiert,
Waar in de Godsdienst word, naar **ENG'LANDS** trant, geviert,
Is fraai en lovenswaard. Nu elders heen getreden.
Hier zie 'k de **KERK**, waarin, naar Duitsche taal en zeden,
De Godsdienst word geleerd. Wat verder zie ik 't gesticht
Der **NIEUWE KERK**, waarin, Gods heilwoord, naar het licht
Van 't Euangely word ontvouwt aan elks gedachten.
ô Heerlyk timmerwerk, om uwen stant hoog te achten!
Strek eeuwen lang 't cieraad van Leyden; dat zo trouw
Zyn tyd en vlyt en geld bestede aan uwen bouw.
Ik heb geen stof om van de **LOOTSKERKE** iets te reppen.
Nu 't my gebeuren mag myn adem weêr te scheppen

<meta>catchword: Op</meta>

<column-break/>

Op 't vlakke land, neem ik, ô Leyden! met deez' wensch
Van u myn afscheid: dat nooit tyd uw roem verlensch':
Uw welvaart groeije en bloeije, in wederwil der jaaren:
De Zon van uw geluk duik' nimmer in de baaren
Van druk noch tegenspoed; maar straale, al 't Land ten troost,
In ongestoorden loop uit een gezegent Oost.
Nu roept my 't **PESTHUIS**, dat, byna een eeuw geleden,
Gebouwt, door 't wyz' beleid van Leydens Overheden,
Niet weinig aanziens heeft. Hier worden, wen de dood,
Door 't Pestvuur, hevig woed, en dreigt met zwaaren nood
De Inboorelingen, hen een goed verblyf gegeeven,
Die in gevaar zyn om door zulk een kwaal te sneeven.
Nu strekt het ten verblyf van zieke en arme Liên.
Nooit moet ge, ô Leyden! aan dit Huis het onheil zien,
Dat laatst het Pesthuis moest van Amsteldam bezuuren;
't Geen in één nacht verbrand, alleenig zyne muuren
Voor 't vuur bewaaren zag. Doch treên we verder voort.
ô Heuglyk **TUINGEZICHT**, dat, by de **MAREPOORT**,
Langs Haarlems Trekvaart is te zien! gy streelt myn zinnen.
Wie can uw fraaiheid en vermaaklykheid ontginnen?
Myn veder is te zwak, en mynen geest te kleen.
Een ander **TUINGEZICHT** lokt my weêr elders heen,
Dat, **AAN DEN RHYN** zich koomt ontdekken aan myn oogen.
Hier ziet men Jachten, door den koelen wind bewoogen,
Spanfeeren langs uw rug, ô aangenaame stroom!
Dien vader Vondel achte als zynen zoetsten droom,
In 't onnavolgbaar dicht, zo schoon, zo onbedwongen,
En zielverrukkende tot uwen roem gezongen.
Maar noch veel fraayer toont ge, ô **RHYN**! u in 't verschiet,
Daar myn nieuwsgierig oog, u by de **ZYLBRUG** ziet.
ô Aangenaam vertoog! hoe streelt ge myn gedachten!
Wie moet uw fraaiheid niet verheffen en hoog achten?
Waar ik myn oogen wend of keer, ik zie ze blind;
't Zy ik den Hengelaar, die zyn genoegen vind,
Zo hy een vischje mag verschalken, koom beschouwen:
Het zy ik my vermaake in keurige Gebouwen
En Lustpriëelen, die den Tuinen tot sieraad
Verstrekken; of het zy ik de oogen vrolyk laat
Aen de een en d'and're kant van uwe boorden weyden;
Of 't zy 'k van ver begluur het schoon en fierlyk Leyden.
ô Lieflyk Rhyngezicht, en Lusttoonneel van weeld'!
Nooit hebt ge mynen geest met meer vermaak gestreelt.
Maar 'k moet met tegenzin my elders heen begeeven,
Terwyl gy eindloos zult in myn gedachten zweeven.
Het **HUIS TER MEY**, het welk een uwer Raaden hoord,
De Heer van **LANDSCHOT**, trekt me, ô Leyden! zagjes voort.
Hoe fraai vertoont het zich uit eenen reeks van boomen!
Wat is 't my een vermaak om u te wellekomen,
Wyl ik het honk haast zie van d'aangevange reis!
Maar wie verheft u, naar uw voeglykheid en eisch?

The valiant **WILLIAM**, Prince of the widely famous Orange,
Who liberated the Netherlands, in spite of Spain,
From the unbearable yoke of slavish tyranny,
And from the bonds of the tyranny of conscience.
The sciences are reborn in your circle.
Gamaliels <note>A reference to the biblical teacher of Paul, signifying learned scholars or theologians.</note> make themselves heard in you constantly,
And raise, not only for Church, and City and State,
But for all the Earth a series of Men, early and late;
Of Men, who make your fame grow more and more.
Always must you, oh University! flourish through Men of Letters,
Whose praise dulls all other praise, as it always did,
Of all who ever devoted their diligence to Letters.
Now it pleases me to view the **CHURCH OF PETER** <note>Pieterskerk, a historic church in Leiden</note>.
This Church foundation need not yield in beauty
To any building with which a City in Holland boasts.
Its splendor and luster, in which the curious eye wanders,
Charms me! It must preserve its standing for a long time.
The **CHURCH OF THE HIGHLAND** <note>Hooglandse Kerk</note>, one of your Main Buildings
Oh Leyden! draws me forward: There I see the beautiful foundation,
That came so gloriously into the light four centuries ago!
Its luster, elegance, and standing can please my spirit.
The **LADY CHURCH** <note>Vrouwenkerk</note>, which appeared later,
And is smaller, does not need to yield in neatness and ornament
To any Church of the Dutch State.
I go toward the **HOSPITAL**, named after Saint **CATHERINE**:
Here the sick, weary and exhausted by pain,
Are refreshed, cherished, healed, and restored;
And he, whom Poverty holds gripped in its bonds,
Is satiated here, and provided with roof and clothing,
While the Church serves them, to hear the true word of the Lord,
So that the soul, as little as the body,
Lacks its nourishment, and remains not wanting for comfort.
Love for the benefit of each must always make your heart glow,
Oh people of Leiden! thus shall the Divinity watch
Over the welfare of your City, and Religion, as before.
Now once entered into the **BEGUINAGE** <note>Beggynhof, a residential court for pious women</note> of the Maidens,
Who, according to the Roman way, pasture the Church, their chastity,
Or formerly, out of Superstition, led a solitary life;
Its standing is pleasant; and the **CHURCH**, which adorns the Court,
In which Religion is celebrated according to the manner of **ENGLAND**,
Is beautiful and praiseworthy. Now stepped elsewhere.
Here I see the **CHURCH**, in which, according to German language and customs,
Religion is taught. Somewhat further I see the foundation
Of the **NEW CHURCH**, in which God's holy word is unfolded,
According to the light of the Gospel, to everyone's thoughts.
Oh glorious carpentry, highly to be esteemed for your standing!
Be for centuries long the ornament of Leyden, that so faithfully
Spent its time and diligence and money on your construction.
I have no material to mention anything of the **PILOT'S CHURCH**.
Now that it may happen to me to catch my breath again

<column-break/>

On the flat land, I take, oh Leyden! with this wish
My farewell from you: that time may never shorten your fame:
May your prosperity grow and flourish, in spite of the years:
May the Sun of your happiness never dive into the waves
Of pressure or adversity; but shine, for the comfort of the Land,
In an undisturbed course from a blessed East.
Now the **PEST HOUSE** <note>Pesthuis, a historic plague hospital</note> calls me, which, built almost a century ago,
Through the wise policy of the Authorities of Leyden,
Has no little appearance. Here, when death,
Through the Plague-fire, rages violently, and threatens with heavy need
The inhabitants, they are given a good residence,
Who are in danger of perishing through such an ailment.
Now it serves as a residence for sick and poor People.
Never must you, oh Leyden! see in this House the misfortune
That the Pest House of Amsterdam last had to suffer;
Which burned in one night, and saw only its walls
Preserved from the fire. But let us step further.
Oh memorable **GARDEN VIEW**, which, by the **MARE GATE** <note>Marepoort</note>,
Along the Haarlem Tow-path is to be seen! You caress my senses.
Who can mine your beauty and enjoyableness?
My quill is too weak, and my spirit too small.
Another **GARDEN VIEW** lures me elsewhere again,
Which, **BY THE RHINE**, comes to reveal itself to my eyes.
Here one sees Yachts, moved by the cool wind,
Running along your back, oh pleasant stream!
Which father Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel, the most famous 17th-century Dutch poet</note> deemed his sweetest dream,
In the inimitable poem, so beautiful, so unforced,
And soul-ravishingly sung to your glory.
But even much more beautifully do you show yourself, oh **RHINE**! in the distance,
Where my curious eye sees you by the **ZYL BRIDGE**.
Oh pleasant demonstration! How you caress my thoughts!
Who must not exalt your beauty and esteem it highly?
Wherever I turn or twist my eyes, I see them blinded;
Whether I come to contemplate the Angler, who finds his pleasure,
If he may deceive a little fish;
Whether I amuse myself in elegant Buildings
And Pleasure-pavilions, that serve as ornament to the Gardens;
Or whether I let the eyes joyfully pasture
On the one and the other side of your banks;
Or whether I glimpse from afar the beautiful and proud Leyden.
Oh lovely Rhine-view, and Pleasure-scene of wealth!
Never have you caressed my spirit with more pleasure.
But I must reluctantly betake myself elsewhere,
While you will endlessly hover in my thoughts.
The **HOUSE TER MEY**, which belongs to one of your Councilors,
The Lord of **LANDSCHOT**, draws me, oh Leyden! softly forward.
How beautifully it presents itself from a series of trees!
What a pleasure it is for me to welcome you,
While I soon see the home of the begun journey!
But who elevates you, according to your appropriateness and demand?

<summary>The author continues their poetic tour of Leiden, describing its religious, charitable, and public institutions, before proceeding to the gardens and riverscapes along the Rhine.</summary>

Fourth, [a person] omits theft by despoiling the republic, and this is called <term>peculatus</term> <gloss>embezzlement of public funds</gloss>, as in the 22nd Question, 3rd Chapter, "Quod g.," where it is added: "Embezzlement, indeed, is theft from the republic." It follows that it is not indicated as theft of private property, but of the public. Therefore, it is asked what is to be said regarding those who turn public monies or other public things into their own. To this it must be said that, beyond [the fact that] things should be punished by capital penalty according to the laws, as in the Institutes, "De publicis iudiciis," the Julian Law of Embezzlement, because he who mixes iron or similar [materials] with public gold or silver [is guilty]. As in the final law, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, a public moneyer who stamps public currency and retains [some] for himself, as in the law "Sacrilegis," chapter of the same. Public officials who hold the seal and do not account for the florins, and these [men] damaging the republic, fall into embezzlement, as in the argument regarding the law "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, he who damages the republic by damaging or changing a book or writing concerning the measurement of fields or a public road, as in the law "Quod tabulas," in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, he who damages the republic by feigning creditors of the treasury and receiving money from the treasury which should be private property, as in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus," law "Sacrilegis," of the same chapter. Similarly, public officials selling [offices] and dictators are held to restitution of money, even if not to those who gave [it], if they are poor, and those purchasing illicitly wish to be punished by the gravity of the Julian Law on Bribery, law "Unica," in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam ambitus," Institutes "De publicis iudiciis." [These are the things] furthermore, and these, for their sons, judgment must be had. But those who justly serve the republic, if they were to serve for a time for their own private gain with the monies of the republic, they would not sin, provided that the republic was in no way burdened or suffered damage, for instance, in that it would be burdened for all that time; otherwise, it would remain intact and not applied to anyone or for any utility. For all who bring damage to the republic, for example, by falsifying currency in weight, form, or common standard, or by diminishing [the quality] for gain, or [falsifying] gold or silver, and these [people] and others who are simply purifying [the metal], and those who with various measures, weights, and measures falsify, are called thieves of the republic, as in the Digest, "De contrahenda emptione," law 1; and such thieves are punished by the laws in boiling water, as in the Digest, "De falsa moneta," law 2, and such currency does not deserve to be paid, Digest "De pignoribus," law "Eleganter." In this lot also are counted merchants who agree among themselves that goods are given at a certain price, specifically that many are sold for a higher price, or that only one person may sell certain goods, for those who exercise such an office and those laws should all be despoiled of their goods and punished with perpetual exile. Similarly, those approaching and admitting it should be punished, as in the Code "De monopoliis," law "Una," and it is no wonder, because such [people] most greatly damage the city and are held to the restitution of all that they received for more than a just price. Of which detestable theft it is to move the boundaries of a neighbor, of which it is written, Deuteronomy 21: "Cursed is he who moves the boundaries of his neighbor," which is principally understood as the great extension of someone’s field and the unjust usurpation of anyone’s property. To the praise of God.

Regarding the restitution of theft in the last four modes, namely in sacrilege, in [items] found in the use of another's thing, and in hidden retention [or] unjust [retention of] justly acquired [things]. Sermon 9. <note>Large red decorative initial O</note>On theft, Exodus 20. Having discussed the four first differing [types] of theft, now let us pursue the rest. The fifth, indeed, is the theft they commit by which they incur sacrilege, which itself aggravates the theft not insignificantly, as Augustine says on John, and it is held in the 22nd Question, 3rd Chapter, "Quod g.," which is not indicated as theft of private property, but of the republic, as appears in the following law. "How much more vehemently is the sacrilegious thief to be judged, not just anyone, but [he who] steals from the church, [for] anyone who steals something from the church is entirely to be condemned, because he was a thief of sacred vessels and holy places," as it is promised in the same place. For which it must be known that sacrilege is whenever someone violates the sacred, either by taking the sacred from the sacred, or the profane from the profane, or the profane from the sacred, or the sacred from the profane, as is held in the 15th Question, 3rd Chapter, "Hi quis contumax," question "Sacrilegium," where it is added that sacrilege sustains double penalty, namely pecuniary and of excommunication, and according to the gloss, the first is for the damage suffered, the second is for the immunity of the church violated.

# Gate 9

This refers to the language of the **Source**, from which the word and the mystery are drawn. "A river goes out of Eden" <note>Genesis 2:10</note>—meaning, a river emerges from the Source and the Fountain. The term "Eden" <note>Hebrew: *Eden*</note> is related to the expression used regarding Sarah when her "source" <note>a euphemism for her menstrual cycle/fertility</note> had ceased and then returned to her; she said, "After I have withered, shall I have **rejuvenation**?" <note>Hebrew: *Ednah*; Genesis 18:12</note>. This implies that the Source was renewed within her.

We have already explained that "A river goes out of Eden" refers to the Sefirah of **Binah** <note>Understanding</note>. "Going out of Eden" means it emerges from **Chokhmah** <note>Wisdom</note>, which is the mystery of the Source drawn from the **Supreme Crown** <note>Keter</note>. 

"To water the garden" <note>Genesis 2:10</note> means to provide divine flow to the Sefirah of **Malkhut** <note>Kingship</note>. **Binah**, which is the mystery of the River, waters **Malkhut**, which is the Garden, by means of the seven Sefirot: **Gedulah** <note>Greatness/Mercy</note>, **Gevurah** <note>Might</note>, **Tiferet** <note>Beauty</note>, **Netzach** <note>Victory</note>, **Hod** <note>Splendor</note>, and **Yesod** <note>Foundation</note>. This is the mystery of the seven [levels] that exist between the first letter *He* (ה) of the Name <note>the Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note> and the final *He* (ה). 

From **Malkhut** and below is the **World of Separation** <note>see Sefer ha-Bahir, page 17</note>. "And from there it was parted and became four heads" <note>Genesis 2:10</note> refers to the mystery of the four camps of the **Shekhinah** <note>the Divine Presence</note> that separate from the mystery of the **World of Unity**. This is the mystery of (A) the four letters in Unity, and the "four heads" in Separation.

Now, we must inform you of what is written in the Torah: "The Lord God planted a garden in Eden from the east" <note>Genesis 2:8</note>. (B) How is this possible? For we have said that it [Eden] is the mystery of the world of **Keter** <note>Crown</note>, which is the world of **Thought** that "no eye has ever seen" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>—so how can you say the Garden is planted *within* Eden? 

(C) Furthermore, our Sages revealed this matter in the chapter "One may not stand" <note>Talmud, Berakhot 30b/34b</note>: (D) Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, "What is 'Eye has not seen'? This is the **wine preserved in its grapes** from the six days of Creation." Resh Lakish said, "This is Eden, which no eye has ever seen." And if you ask, "Where did Adam live?"—he lived in the Garden. And if you ask, "Is the Garden not Eden?"—the verse teaches: "A river goes out of Eden to water the garden." Thus ends their words.

Contemplate the words of the Master [the author] of blessed memory in this place. He says that Eden is one thing and the Garden is another. If so, how can the literal meaning of the verse be settled? For they did not finish explaining it in the Talmud. 

Here, I will provide a hint: "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden." He planted the roots of the Garden—which is the mystery of the Sefirah of **Malkhut**—within Eden, which is the mystery of the **Beginning of Thought** <note>Chokhmah</note>. This is because the end of Wisdom <note>Chokhmah</note> and the end of Intelligence <note>Binah</note> are one unified whole. This is the mystery of the "planting." 

How so? The final letter *He* (ה) of the Name has its "plantings" extending into the letter *Vav* (ו), and from there they spread and go until the first letter *He* (ה), and from there they draw nourishment from the letter *Yod* (י) <note>it is known that the *Keter* surrounds the *Yod* and the power of the *Ein Sof* is there</note>, which is the first letter of the Name. This is the mystery of "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden"—it is a great mystery, hidden and sealed within the four letters of the Name. 

From where is all this drawn? "From the east" <note>Hebrew: *Mi-Kedem*</note>—this is the mystery of the **tip of the Yod** <note>representing Keter, the highest point</note>. A wealthy person <note>or a wise one</note> knows how to direct the path according to the order of the Garden's planting, from the level of the Sefirah of **Malkhut** up to the Sefirah of **Chokhmah**, which is the mystery of the True One. (E) ~~Gate of the matters of my handiwork~~ to be glorified. If you understand what we hinted at in the *Faithful Shepherd* <note>Ra'aya Meheimna</note> <insert>Section 100</insert>, the literal meaning will be settled. What the Sages of blessed memory interpreted regarding it also settles upon "Eden to its ground," as a river goes out from it to water the Garden. The truth is that it is so: Adam lived in the Garden, and not in Eden. (F) And the reason is "Eye has not seen." (G) [This mystery] is hidden within many things in Creation; if you are worthy, you will receive a "drop to the mouth" of deep and sealed traditions regarding them, which we hinted at in the word *Adonai* <note>Lord</note>. The things we have written are merely hints and parables. 

The Sages of blessed memory already hinted at great principles regarding this in the Midrash. You must also consider that there is another difficult verse: "You were in Eden, the garden of God" <note>Ezekiel 28:13</note>, which implies that Eden *is* the Garden. I am now untying the knots of doubt: **Hiram**, king of Tyre, ascended in the Beginning of Thought, which is Eden, and he is the "Grapes." <note>Note: 'Wine preserved in its grapes'</note>. And this is a <margin>hidden</margin> matter.

---

**Commentary (Sha'ar Cheshbon):**

**(A) Four letters in Unity, etc.** This means the four letters of the Name [Y-H-V-H] which are hinted at in the unity of the Sefirot. Correspondingly, in the World of Separation, there are the four winds [directions] of the world, as mentioned at the beginning of the Gate.

**(B) And behold, Eden is for those who say** that it is the mystery of the world of **Keter**, because it is the source of the "workings" there, the world of the Crown.

**(C) Furthermore, the Sages revealed the matter.** Meaning, they revealed that Eden and the Garden are two distinct levels: the Garden is one, and Eden is another.

**(D) Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said: "Preserved in its grapes."** The explanation is that **Binah** is called this because it is "preserved" by itself—Keter and Chokhmah—from any [unbalanced] extension from there. "Preserved" <note>Meshumar</note> is from the language of "guarding" <note>Mishmeret</note>. "Eye has not seen" refers to **Binah**, for it is the guard of the "six days of Creation" <note>the lower six Sefirot</note> that follow it. My understanding is only slight, based on the mention of the "dwelling place" as a model of the [primordial] days. It is also called "Wine" because there is a measure of "Judgment" <note>Din</note> within it. The reason for this is that through it, all the paths that are hidden in the mystery are spread out and revealed to the world, just as wine brings joy. It is the joy of the intellect and the connection...

Popular fancy makes Buddha ubiquitous, placing him thereby on a par with an anthropomorphic god, and lowering him to the level of a tribal deity ; and, as a result, it falls into flat contradictions, as in Tibet and China.
